newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian president says Democrats defeated in poll.
newsitem.headline: Albanian president says Democrats defeated in poll.

text.p: Albanian President Sali Berisha said on Monday his Democratic Party had been defeated in a general election at the weekend and urged his supporters to respect the results of the poll with dignity.

Berisha made his announcement before any official results had been declared but appeared to confirm that the rival Socialist Party were the victors in the election called to restore stability after months of unrest.

"Albanian voters yesterday seemingly voted that the Democratic Party should be in opposition. On this occasion I would like to express my deepest gratitude to those hundreds and thousands of Albanians...who supported the Democratic Party," Berisha said in a televised address.

"I invite all these electors, all the members, activists, sympathisers of the Democratic Party to treat yesterday's verdict with courage and dignity and to continue together ...our efforts as an opposition to consolidate democracy," said Berisha, who appeared relaxed in he brief two-minute address.

Berisha said he would respect all the commitments he made before and during the election campaign but it was not clear whether he meant he would step down. Many Albanians believe it is only a matter of time before he goes.
Democrat chairman Tritan Shehu told Reuters: "He has not resigned for the moment. But it all depends on him now."

Socialist Party leader Fatos Nano claimed a sweeping victory across the country a few hours after polls closed on Sunday evening. The party says it has won already 63 of the 115 seats being contested.

With expectations of gaining at least half the remaining 40 seats shared out under a proportional system, Nano said the Socialists and allied leftist parties would hold a two-thirds majority in parliament.

A two-thirds majority would be enough to remove a head of state by parliamentary vote. Berisha, president since 1992 when the Democrats swept to power, has hinted on several occasions that he would quit if a leftist government came to power.
Nano, who was holding a news conference as the president spoke, suggested there might be changes at the top.

Released from jail in March after three years in jail following a suspect trial, Nano said Albania should work towards renewing the country's political institutions "...even to renew the institution of president in the most peaceful way without permitting a vacuum".
"Berisha lost his final chance for cohabitation with the Albanian people and the political forces that represent them," he added.
Interim Prime Minister Bashkim Fino, who came to office in March when a 10-party unity coalition was formed to halt the spreading choas, said the elections were democratic.

Speaking on television before the president's address, Fino appealed to police and state officials to work responsibly. More than 1,500 people have been killed in violence sparked by the collapse of pyramid investment schemes in January.

"I ask all officials of state, the police, army and national information service (the secret police), the republican guard, the courts and state prosecution to carry out their duties with responsibility," Fino said.
The Democrats won most parliamentary seats in the 1996 poll which was criticised by the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) as seriously flawed.

The OSCE, together with the Council of Europe and a 100-strong delegation from the United States monitored Sunday's first round of the election and appeared broadly satisfied with the conduct of the poll.
Whoever is finally declared victor will have a huge struggle in bringing to heel parts of southern Albania which remains in the sway of armed gangs and criminal groups.
